analysis.one_liner: Approves the northern Keystone XL pipeline without a presidential permit, skipping further environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill to approve the northern Keystone XL pipeline without a presidential permit was referred to three House committees and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have declared that TransCanada's northern Keystone XL pipeline, running from the Canadian border to Nebraska's border, needed no presidential permit. It would also have declared the 2011 environmental review finished, satisfying the National Environmental Policy Act by law rather than by review. It left the disputed portion inside Nebraska untouched. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada, which filed the permit application the bill would approve, and Canadian oil sands producers, who would get a direct line to Gulf Coast refineries. Some construction workers would gain pipeline jobs while it was being built.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that no presidential permit would be required for TransCanada's May 2012 application for the northern portion of Keystone XL, removing the executive branch from the approval process for this specific project.

It deems the State Department's August 2011 final environmental impact statement to satisfy every requirement of the National Environmental Policy Act, closing off any further environmental review of the route it covers.
It leaves Nebraska's own ongoing work on the fully in-state portion of the pipeline alone, carving that contested stretch out of the federal approval.

analysis.who_pays: Communities and landowners along the route in Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and the Nebraska border country would bear the risk of spills, including over the Ogallala aquifer, and the larger climate cost of expanded oil sands production. The bill would have stripped them of the chance for further environmental review.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have satisfied the nation's environmental review law for this project by declaring it so, rather than by completing review — a shortcut for one pipeline application filed by one company.

Even if enacted, the bill would not have settled the pipeline's fate: it covers only the stretch from the Canadian border to the South Dakota/Nebraska line and expressly leaves Nebraska's own work on the in-state portion alone, so the hardest routing questions would have remained open.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — a faster approval for a pipeline that would create construction jobs and move Canadian oil to Gulf refineries — went mainly to TransCanada and oil sands producers. The costs, spill risk to land and water along the route and the certainty of the environmental review process being waived by statute, fell on the public. It was a targeted fix for one applicant rather than a general permitting reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and two of their subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up; it died when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Lee Terry of Nebraska introduced the bill on July 23, 2012, with 54 cosponsors — 53 Republicans and one Democrat — and it was immediately referred to three committees.
Within days it was passed down to the Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials subcommittee and the Energy and Power subcommittee, and the record of action ends there.
No committee reported the bill, no chamber voted on it, and the 112th Congress ended without any further action on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill mainly served TransCanada and oil sands producers, its death in committee meant no law was passed approving the pipeline while waiving environmental review — a relative gain for landowners and communities along the route, though the pipeline fight continued in other bills and in the permitting process itself.

for.name: Rep. Lee Terry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to approve the northern Keystone XL pipeline without a presidential permit.

for.name: TransCanada Corporation
for.what_they_did: Filed the May 2012 permit application the bill would approve; the bill is written around that single application.

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup or floor action; the record ends with subcommittee referrals in July 2012.

sides.party_line_note: All but one of the bill's 55 initial cosponsors were Republicans (Rep. Matheson of Utah was the lone Democrat), and the bill died in committee without a floor vote in a chamber the same party controlled.

industries.note: The bill was written to approve TransCanada's own application and waive further environmental review for its northern route. The public would carry the spill and climate risk while the company got a guaranteed approval without going back through the permitting process.
A direct line from Alberta to Gulf Coast refineries would expand the market for oil sands crude. Expanded oil sands production is a major source of the carbon emissions the public otherwise bears.
Refineries built to process heavy Canadian crude would get cheaper, more reliable feedstock. Any savings at the pump for consumers would be modest and indirect.
